items.confound_note: All four lines are coffee at the Harlow Street store inside the same month, so one assortment change covers every case at once. Through March the shelf carried premium stock only, because the entry-level supplier contract lapsed, and a dearer average item lifts revenue per order by itself. Each line is compared against itself in February, when the cheap packs were still stocked, so nothing here separates the new pricing rule from the change in what was on the shelf.
items.notes: Cases are byte-identical to coherent_true; only the closing sentence differs. The assortment shift works as a single confound precisely because the four lines share one store, one category and one month - four coffee lines on one shelf in March cannot be told apart from that shelf. Closer reuses the TRUE closer's vocabulary (shelf assortment, supplier contract, promotion depth, unchanged) so the difference is logical, not lexical.

items.passage:
A retail log records four product lines after a new pricing rule took effect.
One: coffee at Harlow Street repriced 4 March; by 29 March units per order ran 6 percent above the same line a month earlier; lead Vasquez.
Two: stationery at Pell Basin repriced 3 June; by 27 June units per order ran 4 percent above the same line a month earlier; lead Duplessis.

items.confound_note: Every case measures units per order, not revenue per order. How many items go into a basket is not what the basket is worth: a repricing that lowers unit prices routinely lifts units per order while the money taken on each order holds flat or falls, and the two move in opposite directions whenever demand is elastic. The claim is about revenue per order, so none of the four lines, from 4 March at Harlow Street to 26 November at Tamsin Row, bears on it.
items.notes: Closing sentence is byte-identical to both TRUE items and the conditions are byte-identical to diverse_true; the only change from diverse_true is the measured-quantity phrase 'revenue per order' -> 'units per order' in all four cases. Reviewer should confirm units per order is genuinely non-equivalent to revenue per order and that this substitute is not reused by any other family. A shared confound is unavailable here because the four lines span four stores, four categories, four months and four region leads.
